name: Clinical Case Conference
description: A professional grand-rounds case system with navy bookends, clean diagnostic evidence pages, symptom timelines, differential reasoning, treatment pathways, and action-oriented clinical lessons.
style_guide:
# Clinical Case Conference

## Visual concept

This English-language style is designed for grand rounds, morbidity and mortality review, departmental case conferences, and evidence-based clinical teaching. Deep navy bookends create a confidential conference frame, while warm-white body pages keep histories, investigations, diagnostic reasoning, and treatment details easy to inspect. Cyan marks synthesis and learning; a rare alert accent identifies critical findings or immediate action. Every page should reveal how the clinical team moved from presentation to evidence, decision, intervention, outcome, and a transferable lesson.

## Canvas, grid, and safe area

- Use a fixed `1280 x 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `60–72 px` safe margins. All patient details, doses, test results, reference notes, and confidentiality markings must remain inside the safe area.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–22 px` gutters. Typical layouts are 4/8 patient-snapshot-plus-timeline, 6/6 findings-plus-chart, 3/9 diagnostic-tree-plus-options, and 5/7 care-pathway-plus-therapy table.
- Use a thin top rule with section number and page count on body pages. Keep a quiet case identifier and confidentiality note in the footer.
- Set one large conclusion-led title in the upper quarter, followed by one sentence that frames the diagnostic or treatment question.
- Align cards, timeline nodes, evidence rows, tables, and conclusion panels to shared guides. Use `18–24 px` between major modules.
- Keep the reading sequence explicit. Clinical audiences should be able to distinguish chronology, evidence hierarchy, and final reasoning without guessing.

## Color system

### Core colors

- Conference navy: `#0D2B50`. Use for the cover, final discussion page, selected KPI panels, decision anchors, table headers, and primary type.
- Midnight blue-black: `#071D35`. Use for deep background zones, maximum-contrast panels, and confidential framing.
- Clinical cyan: `#248A99`. Use for diagnostic synthesis, section accents, arrival nodes, selected findings, and secondary data.
- Clean white: `#FFFFFF`. Use for evidence cards, charts, tables, and type on navy.
- Case paper: `#F5F1EA`. Use for body-page backgrounds.

### Supporting colors

- Learning cyan: `#7FCAD5`. Use for italic headline phrases, lesson numbers, and light emphasis on dark pages.
- Alert coral: `#EE3E4D`. Use only for critical findings, active diagnosis, urgent events, or a named action target.
- Clinical gray: `#667386`. Use for body copy, method notes, ruled-out reasoning, and metadata.
- Grid gray: `#D5D8DA`. Use for dividers, axes, connectors, and inactive timeline states.

### Usage rules

- Conference navy and Case paper define the system. Use dark pages for opening and synthesis; use light pages for detailed clinical evidence.
- Clinical cyan marks reasoning and transitions. Alert coral must remain rare and carry an explicit critical or action meaning.
- Use one primary accent per exhibit and directly label abnormal, ruled-out, selected, and target states.
- Never rely on color alone to communicate urgency or diagnosis; add a written label, symbol, value, or line treatment.
- Do not use decorative gradients, rainbow medical coding, or glossy hospital-brand effects.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter`, `Aptos`, or `Helvetica Neue`; fallback: `Arial, system-ui, sans-serif`.
- Use a regular sans serif for large conference titles and a bold weight for diagnoses, clinical actions, and critical values.
- Cover title: `74–104 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `0.9–1.0`; use Learning cyan italic for the middle phrase.
- Content headline: `46–62 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.0–1.1`; highlight one reasoning phrase in Clinical cyan italic.
- Section label: `10–13 px`, weight `600–700`, uppercase with `2.5–4 px` tracking.
- Hero metric: `38–58 px`, weight `400–600`; keep the unit, normal range, and time point attached.
- Card title: `19–26 px`, weight `500–650`.
- Body copy: `14–18 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.35–1.55`.
- Table text and chart labels: `11–15 px`; sources, case identifiers, and confidentiality notes: `9–11 px`.
- Use tabular numerals for vital signs, laboratory results, doses, intervals, scores, and outcomes.
- Do not compress treatment or evidence text below readable size to preserve a decorative composition.

## Layout and components

- Cards use Clean white with a `1 px` Grid gray border, square corners, and no drop shadow.
- Patient snapshots use one large demographic line followed by structured rows for complaint, history, medication, social context, and relevant family history.
- Symptom timelines use one horizontal navy rule, five or fewer nodes, relative time labels, and a distinct alert node for escalation or arrival.
- Vital-sign cards use one dominant value, unit, interpretation, and acquisition context. One high-priority card may invert to Conference navy.
- Key-finding rows use a colored left rail, test category, primary result, and one line of supporting detail.
- Diagnostic-synthesis panels combine findings with plus signs or arrows, then state the working diagnosis and remaining uncertainty.
- Differential trees start from the presentation, branch through evidence anchors, and end in aligned candidate rows labeled working, considered, or ruled out.
- Treatment pathways use a vertical sequence with time stamps, location, intervention, and outcome. Medication tables use class, agent, dose, rationale, and evidence columns.
- Lesson cards on dark pages use large numbered labels, one practice statement, and a brief evidence or process implication.

## Charts and data

- Favor symptom timelines, vital-sign cards, biomarker lines, evidence stacks, diagnostic trees, treatment pathways, outcome KPIs, and therapy tables.
- Conference navy is the primary series; Clinical cyan marks synthesis or improvement; Alert coral marks a critical value, threshold, or urgent decision.
- Every value requires a unit, collection time, specimen or modality when relevant, reference range or threshold, and source in the patient record.
- Trend charts must preserve chronology and show the reference threshold. Direct-label important points rather than relying on a legend.
- Differential reasoning should state both supporting and contradictory evidence. Do not present excluded diagnoses without documenting how they were assessed.
- Treatment tables must reflect the actual case, formulary, jurisdiction, allergy status, contraindications, dose adjustments, and guideline version.
- Distinguish observed outcome from expected effect, association, institutional target, and counterfactual claim.
- De-identify patient information according to institutional policy and applicable privacy law. Do not reuse preview demographics, findings, diagnoses, doses, outcomes, or quotations.

## Page variations

- Cover: full Conference navy background, oversized three-line title, one Learning cyan italic phrase, subtle clinical waveform, conference metadata, and clear confidential marking.
- Case background and presenting complaint: a patient snapshot card on the left, symptom-to-door timeline on the right, and four arrival-vital cards along the bottom.
- Findings and diagnostic reasoning: stacked finding rows and a dark risk panel on the left, then one biomarker trend and a diagnostic-synthesis panel on the right.
- Differential diagnosis and key evidence: a presentation node and dark decision-anchor panel on the left, connected to aligned working, considered, and ruled-out diagnosis rows.
- Treatment and outcome: four outcome KPI cards across the top, a timed care pathway on the left, and a guideline-directed therapy table on the right.
- Discussion, lessons, and implications: return to Conference navy with three numbered clinical lessons, one large institutional implication, and three concrete take-home or action cards.

## Imagery and icons

- Prefer de-identified ECGs, radiology, ultrasound, pathology, procedural diagrams, monitoring traces, or anatomy illustrations that directly support the reasoning.
- Every clinical image needs modality, orientation, acquisition timing, annotation, and source. Remove all embedded patient identifiers.
- Use arrows, circles, or labels sparingly to point to a finding without covering diagnostic detail.
- Keep icons rare and functional. A check, cross, alert, or timeline node may clarify status, but written labels remain mandatory.
- Do not use identifiable patient portraits, sensational emergency photography, decorative anatomy, or stock imagery as clinical evidence.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview case identifiers, demographics, history, test results, diagnoses, treatments, doses, outcomes, metrics, or institutional claims.
- Do not expose protected health information or combine details that make a patient re-identifiable.
- Do not present retrospective reasoning as if uncertainty never existed; show competing hypotheses and the evidence that changed probability.
- Do not omit adverse events, contraindications, discordant findings, missing data, delays, or limitations that affect the lesson.
- Do not use gradients, glossy effects, 3D anatomy, crowded dashboards, tiny medication text, or decorative vital-sign icons.
- Do not claim guideline adherence without citing the applicable version and documenting justified deviations.
- Do not convert one case into a universal treatment recommendation; separate case-specific decisions from broader clinical implications.
